title: Homemade crackers | Houzz Forum
text: Is anyone into making their own crackers? Last week I made crackers for the first time.  They're fun to make.  I loved working with the warm water dough and was very pleased with the results. After making them twice in one week, I bought a perforated half sheet pan, so I am committed to making them regularly and trying other recipes. I'd like to try a cheddar cheese cracker next. Do you have any favorite cracker recipes to share? This is the recipe I used. I'll add the link but this is my tweaked version and it's half the recipe.  It makes about thirty 2x3" crackers.  I served them with hummus for Super Bowl but they're also great on their own. Parmesan Sesame Crackers 1 c. flour (120 grams of King Arthur flour)3 tablespoons finely grated parmesan cheese1 tbsp. poppy and sesame seeds (eyeball it)1/2 tsp. baking powder1/4 tsp. salt (I use a rounded 1/4 teaspoon.)1/4 tsp. sugar 1/4 tsp. garlic powder 1/4 - 1/3 c. warm water (I haven't needed the full 1/3 c.) 2 tbsp. + 2 tsp. oil (You can use garlic oil made by sauteing chopped garlic in the oil in the recipe and straining the oil. I topped my first batch of crackers with Everything Bagel mix but didn't care for the toasted garlic flakes in it.)Topping: Sesame seeds, poppy seeds, parmesan cheese, coarse salt Stir together the flour, parmesan, seeds, baking powder, salt, sugar, and garlic. Stir oil into warm water and add to the flour mixture  in  small amounts. Work into dough as you would a pie crust. Don't try to roll these out on parchment paper--it slides around. Dust countertop with 1 tbsp. of flour. Dump dough onto counter and knead about 10  times. Form dough into an oblong and pat it flat into a rectangle. Roll out  into a 9 x 12" rectangle, about 1/8" thick. Lift  dough as you roll it to prevent sticking. Pick up dough and place on parchment paper. Reshape but don't worry about making a perfect rectangle. Brush top  lightly with a little oil. Sprinkle additional sesame seeds, poppy seeds, parmesan cheese, and  coarse salt over dough. Go light on the salt. Press topping lightly into  the dough. Place on cookie sheet and score into 2 x 3" rectangles. A pizza cutter works well. Prick crackers  with a fork. Bake at 400 degrees for 15-18 minutes. Crackers are done when they are  uniformly golden brown on top and bottom. Watch carefully the last few minutes. Remove any outer  crackers that are browning faster. If crackers aren't crisp enough, they can be recrisped in the oven. https://www.tasteofhome.com/recipes/parmesan-sesame-crackers/

title: Miele Dishwasher F12 F13 Error Code | Houzz Forum
text: I recently had the F12 and F13 error codes on my Miele dishwasher.  The fix was changing the water supply hookup. It was originally pulling the water supply from the hot water connection of my sink.  After testing the water temperature, I found out I had my water heater set too high.  Miele can only be hooked up to hot water if the temperatures do not exceed 140 degrees F.  I moved the supply line to the cold water connection and the error code has gone away. Miele has a built in water heater so it does not need to be hooked up to hot water.  (User manual states either hookup is fine as long as hot temperature does not exceed 140 degrees).  It is also more energy efficient hooked up to cold water because it will not constantly be using hot water if cold is called for in the cycle.

The acid fights the sweet  They needed eating, though, so the other day I did them with vegan salty spread (i.e., emulsified oil and water that doesn't need seasoning), with a decent whiff of "pie spice".  It was a freebie jar.  I generally use it for new recipes that call for "pie spice", and require so little it's not worth mixing up from scratch.  It was perfect on the ravioli.  An essence of that spice flavor without enough to make it cloying.  Really good! Then I got emboldened.  I had portobello ravioli, which plays better with tomatoes, but isn't enhanced by it.  So I made more of a glaze than a sauce of the same salty vegan spread with a good dollop of jarred plum sauce, and a slice of pepper jack melted over the whole thing.  So good! title: Back from Italy! | Houzz Forum
text: DS (31) accompanied me, and we had a fabulous time! I started thinking about this trip as a 'sticking my toe in' kind of beginning to some solo travel because DH's lung condition keeps him from being able to fly (no idea if that will ever change). Between his health difficulties, our terrible car accident, my mother's death, and the pandemic, life has been hard for awhile now, and I'd decided I was going to start traveling -even if I had to go on my own. I mentioned this to my son and when he said, "I'll go with you," I started planning seriously. We had SUCH a great time.  We spent three nights in Rome, then took the train to Venice (where we spent the next two nights), and then took a train to Florence for the remaining two nights. Early Saturday morning, we took a 7 a.m. train from Florence to FCO airport in Rome. Selecting hotels that were within walking distance of the train station worked out really well. The food everywhere was outstanding (my son claimed one squash pasta dish was the best meal he's had in a year), the hotels were terrific, I loved the trains -but I think the highlight was the people. They were SO gracious throughout. Just incredibly accomodating and pleasant. It was a bit of culture shock when we arrived back at the international terminal in ATL, and were barked at repeatedly, "People, one line!" etc. On the way there, son missed his Denver to ATL flight, and had to be rerouted through Amsterdam to Rome, so I ended up flying ATL to Rome myself. Despite my lack of experience, after arriving at FCO, in I was in a cab on my way to my hotel less than thirty minutes. The process was so smooth and the signage was brilliant. We walked at least 7 miles every day and more than 10 on some days, so lots of good exercise., thank goodness because I imbibed in lots of pastries, gelato, pizza and aperol spritzes! Thanks to everyone for the tips in planning this wonderful trip.

title: Martha's Spinach Folly | Houzz Forum
text: I have had a dramatic change in my life situation, as many might be aware. So, I have left medicine, gotten divorced, and am living with and caring for my mother on the 11+ acres we've owned for 50+ years. I am developing both vegetable gardens and pollinator habitat throughout the property. One of my fun goals for this spring is to plant and grow as much spinach as I can possibly manage, since everyone in our family loves everything spinach. I want to make spanikopita, spinach dip, quiches, vegetarian lasagna, etc. My plan is to dehydrate as much as I can, since that worked well this year, on a smaller scale. So, yesterday, I was asking my mom what her first choice/favorite thing would be to have planted in a garden. She said she always enjoyed the first few sugar snap peas, but didn't really need more than a few. I asked if she was looking forward to spinach, and in what form. She said, and I quote, "You mean Martha's Folly?" Apparently, she doesn't believe that it is possible to grow the quantities of spinach I have in mind. I don't know how she thinks grocery stores manage to maintain their supplies, but I am clearly not up to the job. It doesn't matter that she complained all summer about the excessive quantities of succulent tomatoes and peppers, and the bowls of sugar snap peas that went into the compost pile. It's disheartening, to say the least, when you give up your previous comfortable (though also tortuous) life and set out on a new path, only to have those you count on to support you, belittle your efforts. Sorry to whine, but I thought I might find at least a few sympthetic ears here. I will continue on my quest. Fortunately, I had the opportunity to visit with my son this week (before the Folly comment occurred) and he mentioned spontaneoulsy that feeding my loved ones is my "Love Language." (Of course I had brought him a care package of  homemade green tomato salsa, applesauce, dehydrated mangos, and cherry oatmeal cookies). Not to mention the fact that the skills of small scale food prodection and preservation have been lost to a large swath of society, and deserve to be retained and passed on. Anyone heard of the "Local Food Movement?" Blah, blah, blah. Of course my mother is ignorant, but it hurts to have her so oblivious to the value of what I am striving to do. Then again, I'm 57 years old. Why should I care what she thinks? Though she is paying the bills, while I do the laundry, etc. End of rant. This weekend, I will begin filling seedling trays in preparation for starting tomatoes, tomatillos, peppers, etc. Martha

title: Before & After: A double-fronted family home | Houzz Forum
text: The original dwelling of Albie’s House, located in the vibrant suburb of Northcote, was two separate dwellings that have now been renovated to create a double-fronted family home. The clients came to Rebecca Naughtin Architect with an open-minded and sustainably conscious design brief, with an overarching idea of creating a large open-plan kitchen and living area for the family to enjoy.   The footprint of the building remained the same and the two apartments were combined to create a more practical family home.           Each apartment had exhausted 1950s European-style interiors, however, when combined, their exterior maintained heritage significance. The prioritization of the restoration of the front rooms and street façade was of great importance to both the clients and the architect. The front facade commends its original heritage design, whilst traditional terrace archways and elegant cornice detailing were retained and upgraded within the renovated dwelling.     As the clients, one being an author, loved reading and writing, books became a great design initiative and spectacle, especially around the new staircase which replaced the old timber spiral stair.     The new spaces were designed to maximise exposure to the north sun whilst design features such as solar panels and hydronic heating was used to further enhance the dwelling's sustainability qualities. The north-facing garden and decking area are new family-friendly space that allows for indoor-outdoor living with a great connection to the garden from the new indoor living spaces.         From the street, the original Victorian dwelling remains, but the renovated spaces have transformed the two-unit interior into a comfortable, light-filled, easy-to-maintain space for a family to enjoy.

title: Why are Cabinets Important in the Bathroom? | Houzz Forum
text: “Can I see your bathroom?” Such question is rarely asked whether you receive visitors in your home or become a visitor yourself. While this area is one of the most important areas of a home, very few, or no one, will voluntarily ask to check what the bathroom looks like. Often, people would be more interested in your living area, kitchen, or bedroom. Now, the question is: if no one cares, why do you even need to beautify your bathroom? There are several reasons why you should still make your bathroom look pleasant. But the most important one would be because your bathroom is where you start and end your day. When you wake up in the morning to prepare (let us say, for work), one of the first things you would probably do is go to the bathroom. This is where you take a bath, put on your makeup, style your hair, etc. The same goes when you go home: your bathroom is where you will change your clothes, wash your face or body, brush your teeth, and so forth. Now that you already know how vital bathrooms can be, you may wonder how you will beautify this area in your home. There are ways to make your bathroom more appealing and comfortable. You can apply a fresh coat of paint that will fit your vibe. You may also add plants or lights to make it more suitable for a vanity space. But do you know what will truly help you upgrade your bathroom? Cabinets. The Importance of Cabinets in the Bathroom Before searching the internet for bathroom cabinet ideas, you must first understand the benefits of cabinets in your toilet and washroom area. You have to know that while your main goal is to enhance the look of your bathroom, you do not have to sacrifice its functionality, which can be achieved by simply installing cabinets. Here are some reasons why cabinets are important in the bathroom: ● Space saver If there is one thing cabinets are guaranteed to do, it is to save space. This is extremely helpful for bathrooms with limited spaces. By installing cabinets in your bathroom, you can devote a storage space for things like towels, hair dryers, spare toilet paper rolls, and other toiletries. ● Low cost One of the reasons why some homeowners are having second thoughts about installing cabinets is the cost, which is understandable. There is no denying that some cabinets are quite expensive. However, if you search the market properly, you will find that there are different cabinet types, each of which comes at different prices. Cabinet prices may also depend on its material, size, and function. But you do not have to worry about not getting a suitable cabinet. As mentioned, cabinets are versatile storage spaces, and you will surely find something that will meet your needs and fit the vibe of your bathroom. ● Practicality Again, the reason why you are getting a cabinet is to save space. But from a practical standpoint, cabinets make much more sense than leaving your things cluttered in the bathroom. In addition, storing your bathroom essentials and toiletries makes them more organized and accessible. This means you do not have to waste time digging around for the things you need. ● Additional accent to the bathroom Apart from its storage features, cabinets can also add personality to your bathroom. Since cabinets usually come in various designs, colours, materials, and styles, they can be a great addition to the overall look of your bathroom. Some cabinets even come with built-in LED mirrors, allowing them to become multifunctional. Things to Consider Before Installing Bathroom Cabinets Apart from knowing how important cabinets can be in your bathroom, you also have to know the things to consider before installing bathroom cabinets. As mentioned, these cabinets often come in various specifications. Here are some important considerations before installing bathroom cabinets: ● Type When shopping for cabinets, you may think they all look alike. But like what we have mentioned, there are different types of cabinets. There is the mirrored one, which comes with a mirror door along with the storage. This type of cabinet is usually mounted above the sink to assist you with your daily routines, such as brushing your teeth, shaving, and grooming. Another mirror type is the medicine cabinet. As the name suggests, this cabinet is used to store medicine. But you can also utilise it for your extra toiletries stock like soaps, shampoo, or lotions. Compared to the mirrored ones, medicine cabinets can have a larger storage space. Corner cabinets are small compact units mounted on the corner of two adjoining walls. Since they are smaller than the two cabinet types, they are more suitable for smaller bathrooms. ● Size Size is another crucial factor to consider when choosing what cabinet to install in your bathroom. Remember that the goal of the cabinets in your bathroom is to maximise space, and selecting the wrong measurement may defeat this purpose. ● Position Positioning your cabinet will help you utilise the available space better, giving your bathroom a more organised look. ● Material If you want to achieve an aesthetically pleasing bathroom, giving importance to the material of the cabinet is necessary. You can opt for a wood cabinet for a classy and traditional vibe. You may also choose plastic or stainless steel. While these two are relatively cheaper than wood, they also come in different designs that might suit your bathroom’s overall appearance. ● Customisation Ready-made cabinets are available in the market. However, if you want your cabinets to fit the feel of your bathroom, consider customising them. This way, you can experiment with different materials, colours, designs, and sizes. Posted by Rainfaerie               January 22, 2014 CHEESECAKE 9” springform pan with graham cracker crust 24 oz. cream cheese, softened 1/2 t salt 1 T vanilla 4 eggs 1 c sugar 2 c sour cream 2 T sugar First make and bake crust. ALLOW TO COOL Cream together cream cheese, salt and vanilla. Beat in eggs one at a time. Pour into 9” springform pan with graham cracker crust. Bake at 350 F 30 - 35 min. GRAHAM CRUST Pulse 1 1/2 c (12 whole rectangles) graham crackers with 1/3 c butter, melted, and 1/4 c sugar, until combined in food processor. text: 1. Have you ever used bamboo charcoal bags to eliminate an odor?  Do they work? 2. It says to activate them in the sun for 2 hours.  Can that be inside with light coming through a glass window or does it have to be sun outside?  (It is winter, I live in an apartment.) Thanks.  Scoop is below if you have any other suggestions. +++++++++++++++++++++++++ We live in a prewar apartment building.  We've spent three weeks sleeping, working, and eating in our primary bedroom because it is the only place in our apartment that has not smelled. A pipe burst upstairs 3 weeks ago and leaked into a wall cavity next to a closet.  Severely damaged the closet wall.  Our super ripped out the drywall and has the cavity open now to remove moistuer. title: Make-up air for high power range hood in old San Francisco house? | Houzz Forum

I was feeling good about all of this until I started going down the rabbit hole of make-up air requirements.  My understanding is that you need this under the international building code that many cities have adopted once you have  a 400 CFM+ hood  in order to address potential depressurization and backdraft issues. Based on what I am reading, installing such a system seems potentially overkill in our context and likely to introduce new problems with respect to indoor temperature, cost and maintenance. Our house is 3000 sq feet over three floors with many windows and is built in 1904, so I am sure is far from airtight to begin with. The kitchen is in the center-left of the middle floor and has entrances onleading to the foyer and dining room on two sides and is open to a family room on a third side, so (while not particularly large) is not a closed off room. The family room and dining room have two operable windows and a sliding patio door between them, while the foyer is fully open to a living room with a large bay window. The gas furnace and gas water heater are on the ground floor in the garage which has poor insulation and weather stripping and is far colder at night than the rest of the house.  The gas dryer is in a windowless room on the ground floor with admittedly no ventilation outside of the dryer vent. The house is in San Francisco. Does anyone know if inspectors here actually care about this makeup air system concept in this kind of situation? Apart from what inspectors care about, is this something I need to care about in terms of indoor air quality and safety (we have small kids)?  Thanks in advance from any education anyone is able to provide me on this. I am really grateful for the feedback I have received from others on other aspects of this project so far.

title: Penne With Vodka Sauce | Houzz Forum
text: Making this tonight.  I found the recipe some years ago in one of Ina G’s books.  Simple like most but takes a little longer due to the oven time (also ups the flavor IMO).  A few tweaks…I use a 350 oven and often add sauteed mushrooms to the finished sauce.  I‘ve subbed fresh basil for the fresh oregano, too. Penne Alla Vecchia Bettola Serves 4 1/4 cup olive oil2-1/2 cups chopped onion (1 large onion)1 tablespoon minced garlic (3 cloves)1/2 teaspoon crushed red pepper flakes (or to taste)1-1/2 teaspoons dried oregano (or to taste)1 cup vodka2 (28-ounce) cans whole peeled plum tomatoes, drainedKosher salt and freshly ground black pepper3/4 pound penne2 tablespoons chopped fresh oregano leaves, plus extra for serving1 cup heavy cream1/2 cup freshly grated Parmesan cheese, plus extra for serving Preheat the oven to 375 degrees. Heat the oil in a large (12-inch) ovenproof sauté pan over medium heat. Add the onions and garlic and cook for about 5 minutes, until the onions are translucent. Add the red pepper flakes and dried oregano and cook for 1 more minute. Add the vodka and simmer for 5 to 7 minutes, until the mixture is reduced by half. Using clean hands, crush each tomato into the pan. Add 2 teaspoons of salt and 1/2 teaspoon of black pepper. Cover the pan with a tight-fitting lid, place in the oven, and bake for 1-1/2 hours. Bring a large pot of water to a boil. Add 2 tablespoons of salt and the pasta and cook according to the directions on the package. Drain and set aside. Two cups at a time, carefully pour the tomato mixture into a blender and purée until smooth. Return the tomato mixture to the sauté pan (be careful; the handle is hot!). Add the fresh oregano, cream, 1 teaspoon salt, and 1/2 teaspoon pepper and simmer partially covered for 10 minutes. Add the pasta to the sauce and cook for 2 more minutes. Stir in 1/2 cup of the Parmesan cheese and serve hot sprinkle with extra Parmesan and fresh oregano.

title: Trying to get actual facts about quartz. | Houzz Forum
text: So, we are renovating 2 bathrooms. I ordered my vanities through Home Depot, but didn't order the quartz countertops through them, due to cost and limited selection. I shopped around at random places and settled on a fabricator/installer, who sold me remnants. The first bathroom had the vanity installed which was called Callacutta Botanica/Miranda, although the fabricator also called it by other names. Immediately after it was installed, I noticed that the finish didn't seem as glossy as the sample and the slab. I got the sample and there was a significant difference. I contacted the fabricator and he initially said that each slab is a little different. Of course that's why you get quartz, because of the consistency of the product. He then told me, that after they put an additional sealcoat on the courts they must not have buffed it out. That led me to look into putting additional sealcoats on quartz which I've never heard of. This process has led me down rabbit holes trying to get accurate information about a number of things such as putting additional sealcoats on quartz, calling the same piece of quartz by different names, which apparently does happen. I've gotten very frustrated trying to get accurate information. When I have been reading about choosing quartz, I always read things such as make sure it's got approval by the NSF. I've tried contacting them and going on their website and there are no quartz companies whatsoever on their website. I've contacted a number of fabricator/dealers as well as manufacturers and everyone either gives contradictory information won't give any information. So I guess my question is how does someone knowledgeably choose their quartz products. I found out that my piece of quartz came from INDO-American corporation who won't answer any questions whatsoever about anything related to any of the quartz they import. I've been told a variety of things about quartz products coming from other countries such as courts from China and other Asian countries isn't good, but also told it's the same as all the other quartz. Others say quartz from India is inferior. My fabricator is now acknowledging that the finish is different but is blaming my contractor saying the contractor must have done something to it, which is ridiculous. He has said that he will replace it with the same quartz but I'm not sure whether I should trust this man and if I don't work with him I'm not sure who to work with because I've gone to probably half a dozen places and they all give me different answers to the same questions. I've read that there are three grades of quartz top grade commercial grade and lower grade. Some places tell me that's true others say it's not. Some say they're all the same others say some are better at stain prevention than others. I have also been told that some companies such as MSI are actually getting their courts from a number of different countries different manufacturers and that they vary widely in quality. Help! I will post a picture of the countertop with the sample on top of it where you can see the difference in the gloss.

title: How to hand dig, B&B and drum lace root balls | Houzz Forum
text: The following is re-posted from the Professional forum which has fallen into deep slumber: --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------If you visit your local wholesale yard you will see thousands of field grown, B&B stock all machine dug and in wire baskets.  The wire helps to protect the ball from the slings, hooks and fork lifts that we use  to move the plants around. What to do  if no machine is available and you need to  dig a tree?  We have  to fall back on the time honored method of hand digging. A major part of the value of the finishd plant is in the quality of the B&B job.  Here is  how I hand dig a Hinoki Cypress. Materials:  burlap, spade (I use AM Leonard) file, pinning nails,  felcos and calipers.   Tie up the branches, this protects the tree while digging and also while in transport.  Shave off the top until you reach roots.  Define the size of the root ball, you can consult American Standard for Nursery Stock for root ball sizes.   Dig down forming the root ball as you go, cut the roots with the sharp spade, use mattock if you find stones.  Pin on the burlap.  Pin on the top ring of twine.  I usually double the twine for this.  Make the bottom ring and go  all around the root ball.  Remove the nails in the top ring and lace it up as  shown to form the star.  Ball will tighten up with this step.  Break loose the ball at the bottom  by tilting.  If roots are coming  out of the bottom they will have to be cut.  Don't try to lift the ball.  Throw soil under the  root ball as you  tilt from side to  side and the ball  will  rise to the surface, then roll it out.  Patch up the bottom with burlap and lace it up, cinch it up good and tight.  Move with ball cart  or loader.

We had an unreasonably large number of Covid gatherings in the shade of our elm, so welcoming and calming. Elms are also food trees for all kinds of birds, squirrels, and bees.  Important, especially, for birds in the winter who love the tiny persistant seeds.  It was the  tree for entertainment for squirrels and birds alike. title: How often should you change your towel? | Houzz Forum
text: The Importance of Clean Towels Using clean towels is crucial for maintaining good hygiene and preventing the spread of infections. When towels are damp, they create an ideal environment for bacteria, fungi, and other microorganisms to grow, which can lead to skin infections, acne breakouts, and other health problems. Additionally, towels can become contaminated with fecal matter, urine, and other bodily fluids, making them a potential source of infection if not washed regularly. How Often Should You Change Your Towels? Most experts recommend changing bath towels every three to four uses or every week, whichever comes first. According to Dr. Elaine Larson, a professor at Columbia University's School of Nursing, damp towels can harbor bacteria, fungi, and other microorganisms that can cause skin infections, so it's essential to wash towels regularly and replace them when they start to smell musty or look dirty. Additionally, Dr. William Schaffner, an infectious disease specialist at Vanderbilt University Medical Center, advises that individuals who have skin infections or weakened immune systems should use fresh towels each time they bathe or shower to prevent the spread of germs. However, this timeline can vary depending on personal hygiene habits, towel usage, and the frequency of washing. For instance, if you live in a humid environment, you may need to change your towels more frequently to prevent mold and mildew growth. Additionally, if you have skin infections or weakened immune systems, you should use fresh towels each time you bathe or shower to prevent the spread of germs. When to Replace Your Towels Aside from changing your towels regularly, it's also important to know when it's time to replace them. Here are five signs that you need new bath towels: Towels have yellow stains If your towels have yellow stains, it's a sign that they've been overused and are past their prime. Towels are no longer absorbent If your towels are no longer soaking up water as well as they used to, it's time to replace them. Towels have a bad smell that can't be washed out If your towels have a persistent odor, it's a sign that bacteria have taken hold and it's time to get rid of them. Towel color is fading If your towels are starting to fade, it's a sign that they've been washed too many times and are losing their effectiveness. Towels are thinning or fraying If your towels are thinning or fraying, it's a sign that they're reaching the end of their useful life and it's time to invest in some new ones. In conclusion, maintaining good hygiene starts with clean towels. By following these guidelines and replacing your towels when necessary, you can help prevent the spread of infections and keep yourself and your family healthy. text: On Wednesday (I think), I decided to open up one of the cans of 6-in-One tomatoes that I had bought last year to make some marinara sauce.  I had ordered six cans of tomatoes at once, thinking that they would be 28 oz cans, but they turned out to be 105 oz (6 pounds, 9 ounces) cans, and so they each contain a bit over 13 cups of tomatoes each!  When I open one of these cans, I put most of the contents in the freezer, if possible. However, this week, I decided to try storing about 8 cups in jars that hold about 4 cups each, and I put some olive oil at the top to help seal the tomatoes from air and then vacuum sealed the jars.  Then I stored the two jars in the refrigerator in the garage, and I will find out later how this works out.  If it does not, I will not be that upset because these cans of tomatoes cost about the same price as the 28 oz cans, which is why I got confused when I ordered them. I used the remaining 5.5 cups of tomatoes to make the marinara sauce, and I decided to see how it would work in the pressure cooker.  First I sautéed a large onion in some butter for a few minutes and then added 2-1/2 chopped toasted chiles de árbol, some chopped red bell pepper, followed by minced garlic plus some thyme.  I let the garlic and thyme sauté for only a minute or two before adding the tomatoes.  Then I added dried oregano, some San Giovese wine, a small amount of salt, and about a teaspoon of coconut sugar and brought the contents to a simmer. At this point, I put the lid on the pressure cooker and put the pan on my portable induction burner, and set that to cook at 212° for 8 minutes.  I think this must have been too long because I started to notice a scorched smell coming from the pan, and so I shook the pan a bit and turned it off. I noticed that I should not have shaken the pan because some of the scorched tomato came to the top, but it was not too severe, but I was afraid to stir the pan because I expected it to be burned at the bottom, which was the case. I poured the sauce into an 8 cup Pyrex measuring cup (which I had been using for transferring the 8 cups of uncooked tomatoes into jars), and I stopped pouring when I got near the bottom and could see the burned portion.  I discarded the bottom layer that seemed to be scorched (since I had massive quantity anyway), and I tasted the sauce in the Pyrex.  It did not really taste burned but rather tasted more like fire roasted tomatoes, and so I decided that it was okay.  However, the chilies that I added must have been especially potent, as it was a bit hotter than I really wanted. I used the sauce on some fettuccine that I had cooked earlier for some pesto sauce that I had made, but I had made too much fettuccine, which is why it was leftover. First, I had made fresh fettuccine, using two eggs, one cup flour, and 1/4 teaspoon salt.  This made what appeared to me as three servings, and so I held back about a third of the pasta.  The next day I boiled some dried fettuccine, to use up the leftover pesto sauce, and the box of dried fettuccine had 8 ounces left, but I only wanted 5 ounces, which is what I normally cook for the two of us.  However, I decided that 3 ounces was not worth saving by itself, and so I cooked that also and held back one third of the cooked pasta.  Later, I added that to the leftover fresh pasta, and that seemed enough for two servings. This is getting long, and so I will continue in another post.

title: I have few regrets, but ... | Houzz Forum

A few times when I didn't put myself out there to risk the vulnerability of making a friend, or the questions I never thought to ask at the time of someone who has now left this realm. Or maybe I feared looking foolish in front of others, so I refused to try something new.Lately I've been thinking of our trip to Panama, where we traveled to the rainforest to assist in a medical clinic at the edge of the Comarca (the lands occupied by an indigenous community). This was in 2016 and I was feeling a bit shaky after having dealt with some personal issues the year before, so probably not at the top of my game when it came to putting myself out there. It was also miserably hot and wet, and we were among a group of volunteer doctors and nurses, so dealing with a plethora of personalities that were occasionally exasperating.Yesterday I came across the picture below, taken on an afternoon when a group of us walked a short distance into the Comarca to see the beautiful river. It was every bit as refreshingly cool as the photo makes it seem and I felt a tug of longing for that water ... and yet I didn't so much as walk down to the bank and put my feet in. The fear of slipping in the mud and the hesitancy to interrupt the group's schedule caused me to simply look down at the rushing water and capture it with my camera. I still wonder how I might have been changed, even in the tiniest way, had I touched the river and let it touch me.This is really just a reminder to myself to take more chances. Interrupt more schedules. Risk the discomfort of being vulnerable. Go ahead and slip and slide in the mud. Touch the river. Let it touch me.Anyone care to share a similar regret?

title: What size rug do you need for a queen bed? | Houzz Forum
text: A bedroom is a space for rest and relaxation. With the right area rug beneath a queen bed, the room automatically increases in perception of warmth and comfort. When picking out the best, rug placement is a key consideration. The bedframe, room size and shape plus any preexisting furniture are things to understand for your vision to come to life.   WHAT TO CONSIDER BEFORE PURCHASING AN AREA RUG FOR QUEEN-SIZED BEDFRAMES? There are several factors to consider before purchasing an area rug for a queen bed. TYPE OF BEDFRAME Not all bed frames are created equally. Everything from texture, style, color, and visibility are critical factors in choosing an area rug for a queen bedroom set. For frames that sit lower on the ground, a bright pop of color can work against the room and swallow up the furniture. A subtle or pastel area rug may disappear and feel unnecessary for large poster bed frames, lending a sense of chaos or insignificance. BEDROOM FURNITURE Are you building the design in this bedroom around the bedframe? Is the furniture modern, and do you want the rug to help with traditional values, or is it meant to encourage a free spirit? ROOM SIZE The room size will ultimately guide the purchase of the area rug. For queen beds, area rugs under 4×6 will neither add to space nor be visible. Area rugs are traditionally placed under the bed, and certain rooms may even feel smaller after adding an area rug. THE RANGE OF RUG SIZES FOR QUEEN BEDS Choosing the right rug size for queen beds is a simple equation.Bedrooms, on average, are 9.6 x 10 square feet. A queen bed is, on average, 60 inches x 80 inches long. The right area rug for your space should extend 12-18 inches from the frame and leave room for walkability without being touched. Find out how each different rug size for queen beds breaks down below! 4X6FEET RUG UNDER QUEEN A 4×6 rug under a queen size bed is not recommended as it will disappear with your furniture unless paired with a second matching rug. However, using two 4×6 rugs is slightly larger than a 9×12 rug and will take up more space or be challenging to ensure symmetry. 5X7FEET RUG UNDER QUEEN A 5×7 area rug is the smallest we recommend and is great for smaller bedrooms or guest rooms. Due to the length, we caution using dual nightstands or organizing furniture flushed to a wall rather than in the middle of the space. 5X8FEET RUG UNDER QUEEN If choosing to use this size of an area rug, place it away from the back wall and instead lay the rug starting from the nightstands. This simple trick will give the correct length for the rug in the bedroom. 6X9FEET RUG UNDER QUEEN For standard bedrooms, the TSAR design team recommends 6×9 as the best rug size for queen beds. The 6×9 measurement is also ideal for wider bed frames and will provide soft carpeting on three sides of the bed frame. 7X10FEET RUG UNDER QUEEN For larger master bedrooms, a 7×10 area rug will fit beautifully under any bedframe. This size of fabric has the potential to add depth and creativity to a space while not prohibiting other furniture pieces from standing out or blending into the design vision. 8X10FEET RUG UNDER QUEEN The last two area rug sizes will highlight bigger-than-average rooms. Standard bedroom sizes are 11×12, but for these last two area rug sizes to work, the bedroom should be a minimum of 12×12 or even 14×15. 9X12FEET RUG UNDER QUEEN You have two options for laying the rug for either 8×10 or 9×12 area rugs under queen frames. Option one would be to lay the rug under both nightstands and the bed or option two would position the rug about a quarter of the way down from the head of the bed. Option two placement works best with more extended bed frames, including California or Olympia queen frames, or with furniture at the foot of your bed. TRADITIONAL OR CONTEMPORARY: THE TSAR APPROACH While these measurements are best with square and rectangle area rugs, don’t be discouraged from putting circular area rugs in bedrooms. With smaller bedrooms, a circular rug can help to isolate space and give purpose or meaning. For bedrooms that are 10×12, a round rug fits nicely next to the bed frames. For larger bed frames, you can put the area rug at the end of the frame as a creative fringe and injection of personality. Regardless of size, focus on enhancing the space and utilize an area rug to convey warmth, coziness, or flair. With 23 different collections and an award-winning design team, the TSAR touch will stand out in any space, home, or retail office.

title: How to choose the best rug size for king beds? | Houzz Forum
text: Whether styling a project or your home, an area rug can optimize space and aesthetics. Choosing the right rug under a king-size bed focuses on three key details. Don’t choose the wrong decorative flooring; shop confidently after reading these TSAR tips. WHAT IS THE BEST RUG SIZE FOR KING BED? If you have just purchased bedroom furniture, breaking down what will be in the space is essential before buying an area rug. Traditionally a bedroom will have a frame, mattress, nightstands, and a wardrobe. More oversized or master bedrooms will be 14×16 feet or 224 square footage. Important questions are: What do you want the room’s theme to be? Are you looking to keep things simple, or do you prefer a maximalism style? A standard king-size bed is 76x 80 inches long, and a California king-size bed is slightly larger at 72x 84 inches long. With these measurements in mind, you will be looking to purchase an area rug starting at 9′ x 12′ and going up to 13′ x 13′. 5’X8’ OR 6’X9’ When buying an area rug, you have multiple ways to approach the style of your bedroom. For the below measurements, one rug will be used under the king-size bed. If you prefer a smaller area rug, consider a 5’x8′ or 6’x9′, which will only go under the foot of the bed and works well if you have a bench at the end. This smaller rug can add comfort while sitting on this bench or is also great for families with four-legged friends that need a softer walkway on hardwood floors. 8’X10’ Focusing on larger area rugs, the 8’x10′ is a simple approach to decorating and is best suited to king frames that do not have accompanying nightstands. You will be shopping for this size rug if you want to keep the bedroom simple and clean-cut. At this measurement, we do not recommend the bed be flushed with one wall of the room or placed square in the middle of the rug. 9’X12’ With a slightly larger scale of fabric, we encourage one nightstand on this size of area rug under a king bed. title: Wool rugs FAQS (Frequently Asked Questions) | Houzz Forum
text: Wool rugs are best known for their durability and aesthetic appeal. They are also more versatile and easy to maintain; hence most owners will choose a wool rug over synthetic fiber rugs like acrylic polyester and nylon. Check out our FAQs section to learn more about woolen rugs, their features, pros, cons, and everything in between. Wool as a material is one of the common natural fibers used to make carpets and area rugs. Our Wool rugs in Melbourne are durable and flexible for every space. Whether you need a small and soft wool rug for your bedroom or a larger, water and stain-resistant design for high-traffic areas, we have got you covered. All the rugs in our custom Melbourne rug shop meet the highest design quality, and you’ll surely find the best design to suit your unique needs. Check out our wool rug FAQs below to help guide your decision-making. What are wool rugs? Wool rugs are natural handwoven fibers that can be customized to suit different floors and environments. They are resilient to the forces of wear and tear and are the most sought-after type of rugs on the market. Are wool rugs worth the money? Yes. Not only are wool rugs natural and durable, but they also enhance the aesthetic appeal of your space. How can you know if a rug is woolen? Remove one fiber from the rug and hold it using a paper clip. Use a lighter or matchbox to burn the fiber, then check how it burns. If the fiber burns slowly with an orange glow and without any smoke, then it’s wool. It should also smell like burnt hair. What are the main benefits of a wool rug? Wool rugs are hypoallergenic, making them suitable for everyone in the family, including pets. They are also sustainable, long-lasting, and low maintenance. Are wool rugs expensive? Due to their reliability and aesthetics, wool rugs are costly compared to nylon and other synthetic rugs. How long do wool rugs last? With proper care & maintenance, a wool rug can last anywhere from 30 to 50 years. On the other hand, synthetic rugs will only last 3 to 5 years. What makes a rug luxurious? The material used to make the rug, such as wool fibers, and the design often make some rugs more admirable than others. Check out our Luxury Melbourne Rug page for different designs of high-end wool rugs. Are wool rugs itchy? Not necessarily. Wool rugs with shorter and rough fibers can irritate the skin as they rub against it. However, those with longer and softer fibers are very comfortable. What are the pros and cons of wool rugs? Some of the key benefits of wool rugs are durability, color retention, sustainability, and versatility. One of the biggest downsides is the high upfront cost. Does wool fade in sunlight? If you expose your wool rug to sunlight for an extended period, it will fade with time. Do wool rugs smell? Yes, but under certain circumstances. The wool rug will develop an unpleasant smell if it has some mold or mildew build-up. Do wool rugs get softer over time? Yes. Wool rugs will often feel softer with time, making them even more comfortable. Does wool catch fire? Unlike synthetic rugs, wool is flame and fire-resistant. Similarly, they do not melt or stick to the skin when they burn. This makes them a great option for areas with high risks of fire incidents. Are all wool rugs the same? No. Wool rugs vary in quality, thickness, size, and design. The best wool rug for you will depend on your unique needs. Browse through our Rug Shop Melbourne collection to find the best wool rug that suits your taste and budget. Does wool last longer than cotton? Both wool and cotton are more durable than synthetics. However, wool last slightly longer than cotton, provided both are well taken care of. Do wool rugs stain easily? No. Often, wool rugs will repel stains unless they are exposed to stains frequently or for longer periods. They are also easy to clean; hence stains can be removed more effectively. Does wool attract mold and mildew? Wool rugs have fibers that allow moisture to pass through efficiently. This creates a less-than-ideal environment for mildew and mold growth. However, this isn’t to say that wool rugs are mold or mildew-resistant. Proper care and maintenance are still crucial. Do wool rugs ever stop shedding? Your wool rug may shade in the first few months after purchase, but this will stop after a couple more months of continuous use. Vacuuming your rug properly will help stop shedding. Does wool have elasticity? Wool is naturally elastic; hence it can stretch and shrink. The extent of this elasticity depends on the quality of the fiber, the thickness, and the overall design. Can you hose down a wool rug? During a deep cleaning exercise, yes; otherwise, you shouldn’t wet the entirety of your wool rug. This is because you won’t be able to dry it fast enough, and this can cause mold and mildew issues. How can you know if a rug is of good quality? You can tell the quality of a rug by looking at the number of knots per square inch. The higher/more the number of knots, the better the quality. Other factors to consider are the feel and softness of the fibers, how detailed the patterns are, and how rich the color is. Do dogs like wool? Pets love woolen rugs, thanks to the soft and comfortable feel. This also means you’ll need to regularly vacuum your rug to get rid of dog hairs and dander. Are vegans against wool? By definition, vegans are generally against exploiting animals for food, clothing, cosmetics, etc. This means wool isn’t vegan; however, we can’t confirm whether most vegans are against wool. Is wool water resistant? Yes, but up to some extent. A high-quality wool rug repels moisture droplets. It can also absorb up to one-third of its weight in moisture without feeling wet. Is wool rough or smooth? Wool, like cotton, has air spaces, which makes them rough to touch. They also have uneven surfaces, unlike nylon or silk, made of long and plain fabrics. Are wool rugs difficult to take care of? No. If you use the right cleaning components and techniques, caring for wool rugs is relatively easy. You can maintain a wool rug with frequent vacuuming, spot cleaning, and deep cleaning. Can you use vinegar on a wool rug? Yes. Vinegar is great for removing dirt and oil from your stained wool rug. You’ll need to add one cup of vinegar to two cups of water, then apply it to the stained parts while scrubbing it with an old toothbrush or another soft scrubbing element. Can you use/put baking soda on a wool rug? Baking soda is often used as a DIY cleaning technique for wool rugs. And while the entire process can be tedious, it’s a great alternative if you don’t want to use vinegar or detergents. How do you get rid of the musty smell in wool? Use a gentle detergent to wash the woolen rug, then add two tablespoons of white vinegar to the water used for a final rinse. Let the rug fully dry. If the smell persists, wash it again with vinegar until the smell disappears. Do not use harsh/strong detergents or chlorine bleach as they will damage the wool fibers. Can you vacuum a wool rug? Yes. You should vacuum your wool rug at least once every week. Always use a vacuum without a beater bar, as this can cause or expedite shedding problems. How do you clean urine in a wool rug? Use water and vinegar to clean the affected areas. You can also try baking soda, and mild liquid soap. Be sure to mix these ingredients in reasonable, preferably equal proportions.

After wading through all the reviews on the site  I made a few changes to the recipe, to wit: increased the amount of salt, used one half of a very finely diced Vidalia onion instead of scallions and added a half teaspoon of onion powder, used a little more cheddar (roughly grated) than called for, added a quarter cup of grated parmesan, and used the optional dijon (mine was stone ground) but not the hot sauce. For dairy I used sour cream plus an additional tablespoon and a half, as the mixture needed more liquid.  The eggs were warmed in hot water to room temp, which always IME produces a better result in baked goods. I used KA organic AP flour, increased the butter from 6 tbls to 7, and baked them in KA’s own heavy cast iron mini scone pan. The scone pan is much slower to bake; the recommended time for scones on a sheet pan at 375 is 20 to 23 minutes.   I had leftover dough and baked four on a sheet pan for 25 min.  The scones in the KA scone pan took more than 30 minutes to cook, and the bottoms did not brown as much as the sheet pan scones.  Anyway, a great result and I am going to make these for next week’s luncheon.  They are rich and flavorful and the sharpness of that tomato relish will be a perfect accompaniment.

text: Choosing the right carpet and rug can brighten a space and bring life to any area of your home. Check out this article for everything you need to know when picking the perfect carpet or rug HOW TO PICK A RUG There are lots of things to bear in mind when choosing the perfect rug for a room, from material to colour to placement to weave. It can all seem overwhelming when you first start looking through catalogues and websites! In this rug buying guide we will take you through each decision step by step so you can be sure you’re making the right choice. WHICH ROOM? Different rooms need different kinds of rugs. You don’t want to put a thick woollen rug in your hallway as it will hold onto every bit of dirt and mud, making it impossible to clean. High traffic areas such as hallways and kitchens are best suited to rugs that are hardwearing and easy to clean. You might want to consider rugs with dark patterns that can hide stains that you can’t get out. Similarly, you shouldn’t put a hardwearing and coarse rug in your bedroom as it will be uncomfortable under bare feet. Alternatively, you can put super comfortable, soft and high pile rugs in bedrooms and living rooms with lower footfall and in places where you won’t have to worry so much about keeping them clean. SIZE AND SHAPE There’s a saying in the rug industry: bigger is usually better. If you put a small rug on its own in a large space it will give the appearance that it’s ‘floating’ in the middle of some place it shouldn’t be. You either want your rug to go underneath and around all the furniture in your room or, if that’s not possible, to go under the front feet or all the furniture in the room. Depending on the space you might need a square or rectangular rug to do that. Before you look at anything, when you’re at home take a tape-measure and measure out the size you want your rug to be so you know what you’re looking for before you leave! MATERIAL Now that you know which room your rug is going to go in and the size and shape you want it to be, you need to move on to what can seem like the most daunting part of the decision – the material. But don’t worry, choosing the best material doesn’t need to be overwhelming. ACRYLIC Acrylic is both cheap and easy to maintain. It doesn’t shed any of its fibre, so it lasts a long time and you don’t have to worry about losing half your rug every time you vacuum! It varies in quality from soft to coarse depending on how well it has been made, so if you’re buying acrylic look for a rug with a high knot count. Acrylic is hard-wearing, which makes it perfect for entrance ways and hallways. Also, it dyes easily so you can get lots of interesting patterns and colours. Consider a statement rug in the entranceway of your home that really shows off your personality. NATURAL WOOL When you think about digging your toes into a nice thick rug, you’re probably thinking about a wool rug. Wool is super soft, warm, easy to clean and heat resistant – making it perfect to have in front of a fire or beside your bed. It’s also completely sustainable and biodegradable, because it’s naturally farmed. However, all these things make it more expensive than other options, especially for felted wool. SILK There’s a reason silk is associated with emperors, queens and Hollywood stars on the red carpet… It’s because silk is probably the highest quality fabric in the world. All the hard work and creativity of humanity still hasn’t been able to surpass this elegant, beautiful and natural material. The feel is soft and luxurious, and because it’s completely natural it’s much better for the environment than other materials. All these upsides do come with their own problems. It’s delicate, meaning it can be easily torn and if you knock over a glass of red wine or black coffee, it can be easily stained. In addition, it’s the most expensive material on this list. All this means this is not the rug to put in your entranceway. Consider a silk rug for your bedroom, or if you don’t have kids or pets, perhaps your living-room. SILK ‘LOOKALIKES’ – KRISTAL AND TENCEL Kristal and Tencel are man-made fabrics designed to look and feel like silk, but are cheaper and easier to mass produce. Both feel great and are more durable and stain resistant than silk, as well as being easier to clean and care for. Tencel is generally the better quality and more expensive of the two options, but both should be only reserved for living-rooms and bedrooms. PLANT BASED MATERIALS (JUTE, SISAL, SEAGRASS) There seems to be an increasing number of rugs made out of vegan, plant based materials such as Jute, Sisal and Seagrass. They’ve been used for hundreds of years, and although they went out of fashion in the 20th century they’re coming back as, unlike plastic-based materials such as acrylic and nylon, they are vegan and 100% natural, with small carbon footprints. They are cheap and hard-wearing, but very coarse, so good if you want a natural material for a high footfall area like a hallway or entrance way, but not great for anywhere you might be walking around barefoot. They are generally easy to clean, however, Sisial requires a special dry cleaning kit if it gets wet. COTTON There’s a very good chance you are wearing cotton right now – perhaps a soft cotton t-shirt or a nice warm cotton sweater. There’s a reason we use cotton so much – it feels great, it’s natural, cheap and easy to dye any colour you can think of. All this means it’s a great option for a new rug, especially for living rooms and bedrooms where you want to feel it under your feet. The only real downside is that, just like your socks, a cotton rug can wear through faster than other materials so make sure you put it somewhere without too much footfall. CONSTRUCTION Rugs come either in ‘High Pile’ or ‘Low Pile’. High pile is a longer, thicker density option that is deep, comfortable and snug – think about digging your toes into a comfy rug on a cold night. But because it’s thicker, it’s more expensive and it’s easy to get dirt and mess trapped between the fibres. High pile rugs are perfect to put in the living room or bedroom, anywhere that won’t have dirty shoes walking back and forth. Low Pile is cheaper, with shorter fibres that aren’t as comfortable under your feet but don’t hold onto dirt like high pile rugs. They tend to be thin and hard-wearing compared to high pile rugs. They’re great for high footfall areas and places that need to be regularly cleaned like hallways, entranceways and kitchens. PATTERN AND COLOUR What colour and pattern you have on your rug will depend on the material you choose. Some materials, like acrylic, take colours easily so the only limit to what you can have is your imagination. If you have a room without a lot of colour and energy you might want to consider a rug with bold patterns and bright colours to add energy to a room without being overwhelming. Alternatively, you can help to quieten a bright or busy room with a more plain rug in a simple colour. TIPS & TRICKS CHOOSING THE RIGHT CARPET Just like choosing the right rug, you have to think about three important things when choosing the perfect carpet: high pile or low pile; colours and patterns, and material. In this section of the guide we’ll take you through room by room and tell you what to bear in mind when choosing your carpet. An important thing to think about is, do you have pets and will pets ever go in the room you are carpeting? Some carpets have ‘looped weaves’ which can catch on the claws of cats and small dogs and should therefore be avoided at all costs if you have pets (for their sake and yours). THE RIGHT CARPET FOR YOUR KITCHEN It doesn’t matter how clean and tidy a cook you are, sooner or later food will get dropped on your kitchen floor. So you might want to avoid carpet completely around the food preparation area. When buying carpet for any part of your kitchen, choose a carpet with a low pile as these are easier to clean. You might also want to consider a carpet with interesting colours and patterns that can hide any possible stains, and avoid completely pale carpets that easily show marks. Consider Nylon, Acrylic and plant-based materials for your kitchen as these are easy to clean and hard-wearing. THE RIGHT CARPET FOR YOUR STAIRS Stairs get a lot of traffic, all day everyday, so you want low pile and hard-wearing materials like Polypropylene, Nylon, Acrylic and plant-based that are easy to clean. The most important thing to bear in mind, is to avoid patterns on your stairs, as these confuse anyone walking up and down and might cause them to fall. Keep the carpet simple and easy to see the edges. If your stairs are made of good looking wood, consider a ‘runner’ down the centre of your stairs that shows off the wood on each side. THE RIGHT CARPET FOR YOUR LIVING ROOM There will be a lot less footfall in your living room and fewer people walking through with dirty shoes, so you can choose to have a thick, high pile carpet that will feel good under bare feet – consider cotton, wool, silk or one of the silk lookalikes. Because it will get less dirty than other rooms you can also choose to go for a light coloured carpet if you want. A cream or beige carpet can be a great way of lightening a room that’s got dark furniture or walls. THE RIGHT CARPET FOR YOUR HALLWAY AND ENTRANCE WAY The hallway and entrances are probably the most difficult places in your house to choose the right carpet for. It’s the first part of your house guests see, so you want to make a good impression and show off your excellent taste and style, but it’s also the place that gets the most footfall and is most likely to get marked and stained. Because people don’t spend a lot of time in these places, we would recommend practicality and ease of cleaning over picking the most impressive – consider a low pile carpet made from Nylon, Acrylic, or plant-based materials. These materials are easy to clean, hard-wearing and don’t stain too easily. THE RIGHT CARPET FOR YOUR BEDROOM When you get out of bed in the morning you want to be able to push your toes into a warm and comfortable carpet that soothes your feet. That means the bedroom is the part of the house where you can choose the deepest, lushest and most comfortable carpet available. And, because the bedroom gets much less footfall than other rooms, you don’t have to worry too much about wearing through the material, so whenever possible, choose a high pile carpet and opt for cotton, wool, silk, Tencel or Kristal. When choosing a pattern or colour, go for something soothing – you probably don’t want the last thing before you go to sleep to be a bright yellow carpet with orange stripes. title: Lights Flickering on New Build | Houzz Forum
text: It’s a long story, but I want to see if anyone has seen this before. If you like mysteries, this one is for you. We moved into our new build 10/31. We noticed that the light fixtures (not the can lights) would flicker for a couple seconds randomly. We didn’t think there was a pattern to it. It wasn’t when the AC or refrigerator kicked on. It was truly random and it happened at all times of the day. The electrician came out and tightened the screws on the breaker box. The flickering continued. He said it wasn’t anything on his end. He said he had seen it once before where one LED bulb was causing multiple lights to flicker. We didn’t think that was the issue for us, but we had every single bulb in the house replaced anyways. The flickering continued. We then had the electric company come out. They tightened the wires running to the house and replaced our brand new meter with another brand new meter. They ran a load test and confirmed that the power coming into the house was fine and said it wasn’t an issue on their end. The flickering continued. We then talked to our neighbor (we had talked to one before who said he wasn’t having any issues) and found out that he had been having the same problem since he moved in over a year ago. He had a different builder & different electrician, so we then knew it wasn’t an issue with our electrical work. We had the electric company come back out, and they installed a recorder on our meter to see if they could catch any anomalies. We started tracking when the flickering would happen, and we noticed it happens almost every 15 minutes on the 30 second mark and it happens at the same time every day. It got to the point where we’d look at the clock and could count down to when it would happen. It happens on every fixture that’s on at the time. Our neighbor did the same thing, and his lights flicker at the exact same time as ours. The electric company come back out again today to remove the recorder. We shared our findings with him, and he said that was super strange and that a transformer doesn’t have any timed mechanism in it that would cause that. They’re likely going to replace the transformer just to be certain. He said that he has seen once before where this was happening and it was because of a faulty refrigerator that was pulling power from the transformer and making lights flicker. He was confused though as to why ours is on such a set schedule. In that instance, the house was the only house on the transformer. I’m going to propose that the electric company turns off electricity at each house for 15-20 minutes during the times that we’ve for sure seen the flickering to see if possibly one house is causing the flickering. It isn’t our house since the flickering was happening at our neighbors house before our house even started to be built. (If you’ve made it this far, thank you!!) Basically, there are three houses on one transformer. Two of them are seeing the flickering issue. One of them used to see the flickering issue. We’re trying to confirm with him if he still sees it. He was the first house built that’s on this transformer. All houses were built about a year apart & had different builders. They’re all less than three years old. We’re desperate. Has anyone ever seen anything like this?!

title: South Asia Trip report, in multiple posts | Houzz Forum
text: We just got back from our trip, and I realize I never shared pics from our last trip, over the holidays. So I will catch up on that one first. Apologies in advance, there are lot of photos so it will be multiple posts. Our family went to Sri Lanka and the Maldives. Sri Lanka (formerly Ceylon) is an island country off the southern coast of India, similar in many ways to India (a country we all loved visiting). Peaceful, warm people, fascinating culture, architecture, food and clothing. Like India, it has fabulous 5-star hotels, and the ones we chose were all in historic properties. We stayed in a Fort along the coast, where we saw the famous fisherman who fish from wooden perches just off shore. We also saw sea turtles and visited a cinnamon plantation. From there we drove into the interior, headed to the tea plantations. On the way we drove through an area where elephants run wild - you see them munching trees off the side of the road!  And monkeys everywhere. We stayed at two different colonial era tea plantations, in what had been the manager’s "cottages. "The properties were charming with fabulous views and elaborate, gourmet dining. Our favorite parts were a train ride and a seaplane ride. The train we took on New Year’s day, something like 18 stops and 3 hours, slowly wending through the hills of tea country. Our hotel booked us in third class because only those cars have the extra large, open windows (at elbow level). The others are air-conditioned, but the weather was perfect. Given that it was a holiday, the trains were filled with local families. We shared our basket of treats the hotel had packed with our fellow passengers and had a rollicking good time. The views were wonderful and varied. The verdant green hills dotted with women picking tea, the little colonial-era  train stations with flower boxes. Patchwork farms, houses with laundry flying, temples, gardens, rivers, and waterfalls. The tracks wound slowly through communities, close enough to touch, and everyone looked up at the train going by. I made it my personal mission to wave and say hello (Ayubowan, one of the few words of Sinhalese we learned before we left) to everyone. title: Broccoli Cheddar Chicken and Noodles | Houzz Forum
text: Nothing really new but hit the spot last night.  I halved the recipe to try for just the two of us. I found it worked well with less pasta and more liquid.  I added my notes following the recipe. If it appeals, this is pretty much broccoli cheese soup in casserole form with some chicken.  Comfort stuff and DH has asked for a repeat.☺️ Broccoli Cheddar Chicken and Noodle Casserole (From Half Baked Harvest - Serves 6) 1 T. extra virgin olive oil1 yellow onion, chopped2 carrots, chopped3/4 pound boneless chicken breasts, cut into cubes1 tsp. garlic powderKosher salt and black pepper2 T. butter2 T. fresh thyme leaves1 tsp. paprika1/2 tsp. cayenne pepper, or to taste2 cups low sodium chicken broth1 1/2 cups milk1 pound short cut pasta (I used penne)3 cups broccoli florets, roughly chopped1/3 cup grated Parmesan cheese1 1/2 cups shredded Cheddar cheese 1. Preheat the oven to 425°. 2. Heat the olive oil in a large pot over medium heat. Add the onion and carrot and cook until fragrant, about 5 minutes. Stir in the chicken and season with salt and pepper. Add the butter, thyme, paprika, garlic powder, and cayenne, and cook until golden and toasted, 2-3 minutes. 3. Add the broth and milk. Bring to a gentle boil over medium heat. Add the pasta and broccoli and season with salt and pepper. Stir frequently until the pasta is al dente and the broth has been absorbed, about 8-10 minutes. 4. Stir in 1 cup of cheese. If needed, transfer everything to an oven-safe casserole dish. Scatter the remaining cheese over top of the casserole. 5. Bake 20 minutes, or until the cheese is melted and beginning to brown. Serve warm with additional thyme and fresh basil. My Notes: I removed the carrots and onion to sear the chicken, then added them back in. Be sure to season well as you go.  I added the broccoli in Step 2 with the butter, thyme, etc.  She’s a little unclear about the cheese in Step 4. I would add all the Parmesan and enough Cheddar (I used extra sharp) to equal 1 cup. Use the remaining Cheddar on top. I found about 5 oz. of pasta (penne for me) was plenty for a HALF recipe. Maybe 8-10 oz. for a FULL recipe…your choice. See what you think after adding the liquid. I could see more was needed even before adding the pasta. I probably added a full 2 cups broth for my Half version and maybe a cup of milk.  Also, 400 seemed good for the baking time in my oven.

title: Tasty Corned Beef | Houzz Forum
text: Just bought my corned beef for Friday’s dinner.  Been basically using this version for years now.  One of my favorite meals of the year. Corned Beef and Cabbage From The New Basics Cookbook; Serves 4-6 5-6 pounds corned beef (I always buy flat cuts)2 onions, studded with 3 whole cloves (onions can be halved or quartered - cloves optional)4 carrots, peeled and halved2 ribs celery, halved4 sprigs Italian parsley 1 green cabbage (about 3 pounds), cut into 6 wedges (See *Note below)12 small red new potatoes6 small leeks (white part and 2 inches of green), well rinsed (See *Note below)6 carrots, peeled and cut into 2 1/2-inch lengthsSalt and fresh ground pepper, to taste4 T. chopped Italian parsley Place corned beef in large kettle or dutch oven. Add the onions, halved carrots, celery, and parsley sprigs (use seasoning packet if provided with your corned beef). Cover with cold water and bring to a boil. Reduce heat, cover, and simmer for 2 3/4 to 3 hours, turning beef over in broth every 30 minutes. DO NOT allow water to boil again; keeping at low simmer will ensure tenderness. When it is very tender, remove it from kettle and keep warm. Strain the broth and return it to the kettle. Add the cabbage, potatoes, leeks, cut-up carrots, salt and pepper, and 2 T. of the chopped parsley. Bring to a boil; reduce heat, cover, and simmer until vegetables are tender, 30 minutes. Arrange beef on warmed serving plater, and surround it with the cooked vegetables. Ladle broth over beef and vegetables, and sprinkle with remaining 2 T. chopped parsley. Optional - serve with Horseradish Cream Sauce (below). *Note: Keeping the core in the cabbage wedges will help hold them together while cooking. Remove the core before serving. After thoroughly washing, leeks can be tied together with kitchen twine/string; remove for serving. Horseradish Cream Sauce This makes about 2 cups of sauce. The recipe can easily be halved or quartered, as needed. 3/4 cup whipping cream1/2 cup mayonnaise1/2 cup prepared horseradish, drained2 T. Dijon mustardPinch of sugarSalt and fresh ground pepper, to taste Whip cream in bowl until it forms soft peaks. Combine mayonnaise, horseradish, and mustard in another bowl. Fold in whipped cream. Add sugar, salt and pepper. Stir well, and transfer to serving bowl.

title: 5 Main Rose Fragrances. | Houzz Forum
text: I found this on my Canadian website from which I order some roses.  They've put their varieties under rose fragrance categories and there's a delightful discussion about fragrance.  I thought this may be nice for y'all to read.  It quite delighted me. :) :)  Something that would be nice if you could say your favorite roses (any criterion...fragrance, health, whatever) under each category of fragrance. The Five Different Types of Rose Fragrance by Rebecca, Phoenician and our Rose Expert When we plant roses, we think first with our eyes when we consider the color and form of the bloom. Certainly choosing one’s favorite color or the perfect hue for that magical color combination is extremely important. Next, since we’re talking roses, we should think with our noses. Roses are famous for their visual beauty but also their fragrance. Roses can have strong, medium strong, light, or no fragrance, depending on the cultivar. But beyond the intensity of the fragrance roses also offer different types of fragrances to choose from. Let’s explore the different types of scents offered by the world of roses. There are five distinct fragrances used to describe roses: Old Rose is the classic scent that comes to mind when we picture a bouquet of red roses. This is the romantic scent that is beloved in perfumes, baking, and even skincare. The traditional old rose fragrance is warm with a hint of sweetness and is a special scent all on its own. This fragrance can typically be found in red or pink roses. It is the fragrance used in making rose water for which only the most strongly scented roses are used. Fruity fragrance is a broad term used to describe various different fruit-like rose perfumes. Fruit fragrances can include fresh apples, different sweet berries, and zesty citrus. Overall, this scent is light and can occur as a single fruity scent or be a combination of different fruits. Roses with fruity fragrances are an ideal choice for someone who does not like the traditional old rose fragrance. Myrrh fragrance is quite unique. It is typically described as a sweet anise or black licorice scent which is warm and spicy. This fragrance is divisive in the rose community as people either love it or hate it. Myrrh is mostly found in English roses. Though some people might not love this fragrance, that aspect is often overlooked because the shapes and forms of English-style roses can be so spectacular. Tea fragrance is a mixture of fresh tea leaves with warm notes of nutmeg and violet. Apricot and yellow roses typically present a tea-like fragrance. This fragrance is complex in that it can sometimes be a little fruity. Musk fragrance is unique in that the scent does not come from the rose petals but rather from the stamens. One would have to smell the rose up close to smell its warm, sweet, and spicy notes. This fragrance is typically used in perfumes because it has long, lingering notes that can remain present longer than other types of scents. The experience of rose fragrances can be complex. Some roses might offer a combination of these five main types of perfumes. Also, what one person smells and experiences when they put their nose deep into the petals of a beautiful rose might not be the same as the next person. We also all have different olfactory capabilities in terms of the sensitivity of our noses to detect fragrances in general and then appreciate the different nuances within them. Though experiencing fragrance can also be learned. You need to keep smelling the roses! People who are sensitive to fragrance can choose to plant roses with strengths from light to strong while people who have a weaker sense of smell should choose roses listed as having a medium to strong fragrance.
